subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 42-year-old man with a history of daily heavy alcohol use has mild right upper quadrant discomfort. Liver biopsy shows macrovesicular fatty change without inflammation or fibrosis.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this stage of alcoholic liver disease?

options.text: Irreversible regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands
Hepatic steatosis that may be reversible with alcohol cessation
Swollen necrotic hepatocytes with neutrophils and Mallory bodies
Sclerosis around the central vein with portal hypertension
Microvesicular fatty change with hyperammonemia

explanation_correct: Excess NADH from alcohol metabolism decreases fatty acid oxidation and increases lipogenesis, producing macrovesicular fatty change (hepatic steatosis). This is the earliest stage of alcoholic liver disease and may be reversible with alcohol cessation. Alcoholic hepatitis adds swollen and necrotic hepatocytes, neutrophilic infiltration, and Mallory bodies, while alcoholic cirrhosis is the final, usually irreversible form with regenerative nodules and fibrous bands.

explanation_incorrect.A: Regenerative nodules with fibrous bands define alcoholic cirrhosis, the irreversible end stage, not simple fatty change.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neutrophilic infiltration and Mallory bodies are features of alcoholic hepatitis, not uncomplicated steatosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sclerosis around the central vein may be seen early in alcoholic cirrhosis rather than in isolated steatosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Microvesicular fatty change with hyperammonemia is characteristic of Reye syndrome, not alcoholic steatosis.

educationalObjective: Alcoholic steatosis is macrovesicular and potentially reversible; recognize it as the earliest stage of alcoholic liver disease.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 51-year-old woman with long-standing alcohol use presents with jaundice, fever, and tender hepatomegaly. Biopsy shows swollen and necrotic hepatocytes with neutrophilic infiltration and eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions.
question: What are the eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in this biopsy most likely to be?

options.text: Regenerative nodules of cirrhotic liver
Microvesicular lipid vacuoles of Reye syndrome
Copper-associated granules of Wilson disease
Mallory bodies composed of damaged keratin filaments
Lipofuscin granules of aging hepatocytes

explanation_correct: Alcoholic hepatitis requires sustained, long-term consumption and shows swollen and necrotic hepatocytes with neutrophilic infiltration and Mallory bodies, which are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions of damaged keratin filaments. This can progress to alcoholic cirrhosis, in which sclerosis around the central vein may be seen early and regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands lead to portal hypertension and end-stage liver disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Regenerative nodules are the architectural hallmark of cirrhosis, not intracellular inclusions within hepatocytes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Microvesicular fatty change in Reye syndrome appears as fine lipid vacuoles, not eosinophilic keratin aggregates with neutrophils.
explanation_incorrect.C: Copper accumulation is associated with Wilson disease and is not the described keratin filament inclusion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lipofuscin is an aging pigment and is not the swollen keratin filament inclusion characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis.

educationalObjective: Mallory bodies (eosinophilic damaged keratin filaments) with neutrophils on biopsy are the hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 38-year-old man who drinks heavily asks his physician how alcohol causes fat to accumulate in his liver.
question: Which of the following best describes the metabolic mechanism of alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis?

options.text: Excess NADH production leading to decreased fatty acid oxidation and increased lipogenesis
Increased mitochondrial beta-oxidation depleting hepatocyte lipid stores
Reversible inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation by salicylate metabolites
Autoimmune attack on canalicular membranes with anti-LKM-1 antibodies
Impaired copper excretion leading to periportal fibrosis

explanation_correct: Ethanol metabolism generates excess NADH, which shifts hepatic metabolism toward reduced fatty acid oxidation and increased lipogenesis. The result is macrovesicular fatty change that may be reversible with abstinence. Continued injury can progress to alcoholic hepatitis with neutrophils and Mallory bodies, and ultimately to alcoholic cirrhosis with fibrous bands and portal hypertension.

explanation_incorrect.B: Alcohol does not increase beta-oxidation; the NADH load suppresses fatty acid oxidation and promotes lipid accumulation instead.
explanation_incorrect.C: Salicylate-mediated reversible inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation is the mechanism of Reye syndrome, not alcohol-related steatosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Anti-LKM-1 antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis rather than alcohol-related fatty change.
explanation_incorrect.E: Impaired biliary copper excretion is the defect in Wilson disease; alcohol's effect is mediated by excess NADH.

educationalObjective: Alcohol generates excess NADH, reducing fatty acid oxidation and increasing lipogenesis to produce macrovesicular steatosis.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 47-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and low HDL has mildly elevated ALT. She drinks no alcohol. Liver biopsy shows fatty infiltration of hepatocytes with cellular ballooning but no significant inflammation or fibrosis.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition?

options.text: Alcoholic cirrhosis with sclerosis around the central vein
Alcoholic hepatitis with Mallory bodies and neutrophil infiltration
Autoimmune hepatitis with a periportal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate
Hepatic angiosarcoma associated with vinyl chloride exposure
MASLD (formerly NAFLD), associated with metabolic syndrome; steatosis without significant inflammation or fibrosis may regress

explanation_correct: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD) is associated with metabolic syndrome: obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and low HDL. Obesity drives fatty infiltration of hepatocytes with cellular ballooning and eventual necrosis. When steatosis is present without significant inflammation or fibrosis, it may persist or even regress and is usually asymptomatic. Progression to MASH adds lobular inflammation and ballooning with fibrosis that can advance to cirrhosis and HCC.

explanation_incorrect.A: Alcoholic cirrhosis is usually irreversible with regenerative nodules and fibrous bands and follows heavy alcohol use, which this patient denies.
explanation_incorrect.B: Alcoholic hepatitis requires sustained alcohol use and shows neutrophils and Mallory bodies, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-smooth muscle or anti-LKM-1 antibodies and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and would not fit an asymptomatic metabolic presentation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare endothelial malignancy linked to arsenic or vinyl chloride, not to metabolic syndrome.

educationalObjective: MASLD/NAFLD is the hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome; steatosis without inflammation or fibrosis may regress.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity has persistently elevated ALT over several years. Repeat biopsy shows lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning with increasing fibrosis.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected disease trajectory?

options.text: Simple steatosis that inevitably regresses with continued weight gain
Acute alcoholic hepatitis with neutrophils and Mallory bodies
MASH with lobular inflammation and ballooning that may progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma
Reye syndrome with microvesicular fatty change and hyperammonemia
Autoimmune hepatitis that is treated with aspirin

explanation_correct: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is characterized by lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning with progression to fibrosis. It may advance to cirrhosis and HCC. By contrast, steatosis without significant inflammation or fibrosis may persist or regress. The setting is metabolic syndrome with obesity and insulin resistance.

explanation_incorrect.A: Simple steatosis may regress but not with weight gain; obesity promotes fatty infiltration and disease progression.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neutrophilic infiltration and Mallory bodies are features of alcoholic hepatitis, not MASH.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reye syndrome is an acute aspirin-associated childhood illness with microvesicular fatty change and encephalopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Autoimmune hepatitis is not treated with aspirin and would show autoantibodies and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.

educationalObjective: MASH adds lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning to steatosis and can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Alcoholic liver disease and steatotic liver disease
vignette: A 60-year-old man with decades of alcohol use presents with ascites, splenomegaly, and esophageal varices. Liver biopsy shows regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands.
question: Which of the following best describes this stage of alcoholic liver disease?

options.text: Reversible macrovesicular steatosis
Alcoholic cirrhosis, usually irreversible, with regenerative nodules and fibrous bands causing portal hypertension
Alcoholic hepatitis with neutrophilic infiltration and Mallory bodies
Focal nodular hyperplasia with a central stellate scar
Hepatic adenoma related to anabolic steroid use

explanation_correct: Alcoholic cirrhosis is the final and usually irreversible form of alcoholic liver disease. Early disease may show sclerosis around the central vein, whereas established disease shows regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands in response to chronic liver injury. These changes produce portal hypertension with ascites, splenomegaly, and varices, as well as end-stage liver disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Simple steatosis is macrovesicular and potentially reversible, unlike established cirrhosis with fibrous bands.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alcoholic hepatitis is an inflammatory stage with neutrophils and Mallory bodies, not the nodular fibrous architecture described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign tumor in women with a central stellate scar, not a cirrhotic pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hepatic adenoma is a rare benign tumor associated with oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid use, with a risk of rupture.

educationalObjective: Alcoholic cirrhosis is usually irreversible with regenerative nodules and fibrous bands that cause portal hypertension.
